extracted.intended_audience: general readers interested in Christian apologetics and theology (skeptics and believers)
extracted.subtask_description: Criteria and considerations Pascal adduces for regarding Old Testament predictions and related signs as proof that Jesus is the Messiah; focuses on which prophetic features must be fulfilled and how fulfillment functions as evidence. Useful for assessing messianic claims from a Christian-apologetic perspective.

rubrics_metrics.name: Fulfillment of prophecies across ages and peoples
rubrics_metrics.description: An entire nation (the Jews), over four thousand years and scattered books, foretold the Messiah and these predictions were fulfilled after His advent.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Pascal emphasizes the weight of many independent predictions from a single ancient people: 'an entire nation foretell Him before His advent, and an entire nation worship Him after His advent.' The persistence, antiquity and continuity of these prophecies form cumulative evidence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Concurrence of multiple prophetic signs (simultaneity requirement)
rubrics_metrics.description: All different signs given by prophets must occur at the same time for the prediction to be regarded as fulfilled: 'it was necessary that all these signs should occur at the same time.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Pascal argues that timing and multiple distinct signs must coincide (e.g., political history, the seventy weeks of Daniel, and other signs) — the simultaneous fulfilment of diverse prophecies is taken as strong proof.

rubrics_metrics.name: Daniel's seventy weeks and specific chronological markers
rubrics_metrics.description: The seventy weeks of Daniel fix a temporal framework (seven weeks and three score and two weeks = 69 weeks) culminating in the Messiah's death in the last week; the start and end terms determine the time of the advent.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Pascal treats Daniel's chronology as a crucial test: 'Christ will then be killed after the sixty-nine weeks.' The correct historical identification of the fourth monarchy and its chronology is necessary for the prophecy to point to Jesus.

rubrics_metrics.name: Specific biographical and genealogical signs (birthplace, lineage, forerunner)
rubrics_metrics.description: The Messiah is predicted to be born in Bethlehem, to be of the family of Judah and of David, to have a forerunner (e.g., Malachi iii), and to appear chiefly in Jerusalem.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Pascal lists scriptural citations (Micah v, Isaiah, etc.) as discrete markers whose fulfillment is part of the evidence: e.g., 'He will be born in the village of Bethlehem... and will be a descendant of the family of Judah and of David.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Messiah's paradoxical portrayal: humble origin but universal mastery
rubrics_metrics.description: Prophecies represent the Messiah both as poor/lowly and as master of the nations — He is to be 'small in His beginning, and would then increase' and yet 'master of the nations.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Pascal sees this paradoxical set of depictions (the little stone growing into a huge mountain) as a feature that must be jointly satisfied: the Messiah's lowly appearance and eventual universal authority both must be accounted for in fulfillment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sufferings, ignominy, and death (passion motifs)
rubrics_metrics.description: The Messiah is to be rejected, despised, betrayed, sold, spit upon, buffeted, given gall to drink, pierced in hands and feet, slain, with lots cast for His raiment.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Pascal catalogs the numerous predictions of humiliation and suffering (e.g., 'He will be rejected, despised, betrayed... His feet and His hands pierced, slain, and lots cast for His raiment') and treats their fulfillment in Jesus as significant proof.

rubrics_metrics.name: Resurrection and ascension (third-day rising; sitting at God's right hand)
rubrics_metrics.description: He will rise again on the third day and ascend to heaven to sit on the right hand (Ps. xv; Hosea vi; Ps. cx).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Pascal treats resurrection and exaltation as integral prophetic expectations — the raising on the third day and seat at God's right hand are among the signs whose fulfilment supports the messianic claim.

rubrics_metrics.name: Universal recognition and worship by kings/nations
rubrics_metrics.description: Kings of the earth and all nations will worship Him; the Gentiles will be called and come from all parts (east, west, north, south).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Pascal cites Isaiah and Psalms predicting Gentile inclusion and royal homage (e.g., 'Princes and kings shall worship thee'). The broad conversion of nations and homage by rulers are treated as markers of fulfilment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Calling of the Gentiles and overthrow of idolatry
rubrics_metrics.description: Idolatry will be overthrown; temples of idols cast down; heathen brought to true worship; an altar to the true God in Egypt (Isaiah xix).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Pascal notes that conversion of the heathen and destruction of idol-worship are explicit prophetic expectations — large-scale religious transformation supports the claim that the Messiah has come.

rubrics_metrics.name: Establishment of a new covenant and eternal priesthood
rubrics_metrics.description: The Messiah will establish a New Covenant, eternal in nature, and institute another priesthood after the order of Melchisedek which shall be eternal.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Pascal lists covenantal and sacerdotal predictions (Jer. xxiii; references to Melchisedek) as distinctive criteria tying Jesus' role to prophetic expectation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prophecies intelligible to the good but obscure to the wicked (designed obscurity)
rubrics_metrics.description: Prophecies are to be unintelligible to the wicked but intelligible to the well-informed/good; time may be clear while the manner is obscure so only the good understand.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Pascal explains this as divine design: the obscurity of manner ensures the wicked are deceived while the good, by heart-disposition and study, see the fulfilment. He uses the closed mem (numerical symbol) example and argues the balance of clarity and obscurity as explanatory.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rejection by the Jews functions as a test/proof
rubrics_metrics.description: The Jews' refusal to accept the Messiah was foretold; whether they accept or reject, their position provides evidence: acceptance would make them partial witnesses; rejection makes them irreproachable witnesses.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Pascal argues that the Jews' persistent rejection was itself prophesied and thereby becomes a form of testimony: 'The Jews, in slaying Him... have given Him the final proof of being the Messiah.' Their behavior completes rather than undermines the prophetic pattern.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prophecies as the enduring miracle (superior testimony to spectacular signs)
rubrics_metrics.description: Prophecies are the lasting miracles which can be wrought; they endure and are historical tests beyond transient wonders.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Pascal contrasts transient spectacular miracles with the permanence of fulfilled prophecy: 'The prophecies were the only lasting miracles which could be wrought, but they were liable to be denied.' Hence fulfilled prophecy is privileged evidence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Multiplicity of types/roles (comprehensive typology)
rubrics_metrics.description: The Messiah is foreshadowed under many types: saviour, father, sacrificer, offering, food, king, wise law-giver, afflicted, poor, creator of a people, nourisher, etc.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Pascal presents a broad typology ('Types.--Saviour, father, sacrificer...') indicating that the convergence of many different kinds of types in one person increases the improbability of accidental fulfilment and thus strengthens the evidential case.
